title: Best Haul on a Ring
statement:
Stalls stand in a circle. Stall i holds nums[i] coins. You may empty any set of stalls, but never two that stand next to each other. Because it is a circle, the first and the last stall are neighbours too (when there are at least two stalls).

Return the largest number of coins you can collect. With a single stall, you may take it.

examples.why: 5 + 6 would be best on a straight street, but on the ring those two touch. 5 + 4 and 3 + 6 both give 9.
One stall has no neighbour, so take it. Solutions that always drop the first or the last stall answer 0 here.
Only one of the two 10s can be taken; the best partner for it is a 1 on the far side.

hints: On a straight street this is a known DP. The ring adds one extra rule. Which pair of stalls does it concern?
The first and last stall cannot both be taken. So at least one of them is left out. Try each case.
Answer = max(straight-street answer for stalls 0..n − 2, straight-street answer for stalls 1..n − 1). Handle n = 1 separately.

explain.intuition:
The circle only adds one constraint: not both the first and the last stall. Any valid choice leaves out the first stall, or the last stall, or both. So the best ring haul is the better of two straight-street problems: one without the last stall, one without the first. Each of those has no wrap-around, so the usual DP applies.

Inside each straight run the state and recurrence are the same as before: best(i) = most coins from the run's stalls up to i, and best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]). A single stall is the one case where dropping an end leaves nothing, so return it directly.
steps: Define line(lo, hi): the straight-street DP over nums[lo..hi], with state best(i) = most coins from nums[lo..i].
In it, apply best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]) with two rolling variables starting at 0.
pitfalls: Running the straight-street DP on the whole ring. On [5, 3, 4, 6] it answers 11 by taking both ends.
Forgetting n = 1. Both runs are empty and the answer comes out 0 instead of the single stall.
Trying to patch the wrap with a flag "did I take stall 0" carried through two variables. It can be done, but it is easy to get wrong; two runs are simpler.

solutions.title: Recursion with a first-stall flag
solutions.idea: Walk the stalls with a flag saying whether stall 0 was taken; the last stall is allowed only if it was not. No cache, so exponential.

solutions.title: Two straight runs
solutions.idea: Leave out the last stall, then the first, and run the straight-street DP on each.

followups: Do it in one pass, carrying both runs at the same time.
